title: Evaluating AI output
blurb: How to tell whether a change actually made an AI feature better.

slides.title: “It looked fine” isn’t a test
body: AI output varies from run to run, and a change that fixes one case can quietly break another. Trying a few examples by hand misses both.
Evaluation means scoring the system on many examples, the same way every time, so you can compare versions.

cards.label: Spot check
cards.text: Tried three questions — the answers looked good.

cards.label: Evaluation
cards.text: Ran 200 saved questions: 182 correct, up from 171 — but 4 that used to pass now fail.

slides.title: Start with a test set
body: A test set is a saved collection of inputs, each with a way to judge the output.
It doesn’t need to be huge to be useful. It does need to reflect how the system is really used.

visual.caption: Keep adding to it — every bug found is a new test case.

items.heading: Realistic examples
items.text: Inputs that look like what real users send.

items.heading: Hard cases too
items.text: Edge cases, past failures and requests it should refuse.

items.heading: A clear idea of “good”
items.text: An expected answer, or criteria a grader can apply.

slides.title: Ways to score
body: Different checks suit different outputs. Most real evaluations combine them.
Use the cheapest check that actually measures what you care about.

visual.caption: Fast checks for scale; people for the questions that need judgement.

items.heading: Automatic checks
items.text: Code that checks for the right answer, valid format or required details. Fast and consistent.

items.heading: Human review
items.text: The best guide to nuanced quality, but slow and costly.

items.heading: Model as judge
items.text: Another model grades output against a rubric. Scales well, but has its own biases — check it against human ratings.

slides.title: Make it a habit
body: Run the evaluation every time something changes: the prompt, the model, the settings or the retrieved documents.
Because output varies, run each case a few times when results are close.

visual.caption: Look at what got worse, not just the overall score.

items.label: Change
items.text: A new prompt, model, setting or data source.

items.label: Run the evaluation
items.text: Score it on the same test set as before.

items.label: Compare
items.text: Keep the change only if it’s better overall — and check what regressed.

quiz.question: Why isn’t trying a few examples by hand enough?
options: Output varies, and rare failures or new breakages are easy to miss
Models can tell when they’re being tested by hand
It is enough, as long as the answers look good
quiz.explanation: A handful of examples can’t show how often a system fails, or what a change has broken.

quiz.question: What should a good test set include?
options: Only the easiest questions, so scores look good
Realistic examples plus hard cases and past failures
Only questions the model has already answered correctly
quiz.explanation: Realistic cases show typical quality; hard cases and past failures catch regressions.

quiz.question: What’s the main caution when using a model as a judge?
options: It’s too slow to be useful
Its scores should be checked against human judgement, because it can be biased or wrong
quiz.explanation: A model judge is useful at scale, but it needs checking against people before you rely on it.
